title: Rancho Has Kids Now: Rajkumar Hirani Confirms the '3 Idiots' Sequel Nobody Expected
excerpt: Fifteen years later, the three idiots are married, raising children, and staring down a mid-life crisis — and Hirani promises 'a big message' all over again
body:
Somewhere between the engineering entrance exams and the inspirational WhatsApp forwards, **3 Idiots** stopped being a movie and became a generational religion. Seventeen years after its release, it's still the film every Indian parent and child can agree on — the rare Bollywood product that played as well in Beijing as it did in Bhopal.

Now **Rajkumar Hirani** has confirmed he's writing the sequel. And the pitch is devastatingly simple: what happened to Rancho, Farhan, and Raju after the credits rolled?

The answer, it turns out, is exactly what happened to everyone who watched them.

## Married, With Kids, and Questioning Everything

Speaking to *Variety India* and *The Hollywood Reporter India* in separate interviews this week, Hirani laid out the premise with the same disarming honesty that made the original work.

> "It's primarily about what happens to these characters 15-20 years later. It's not about college or anything. They are married and have children now. They are experiencing mid-life crisis, and so we will have to see — now what next?" — Rajkumar Hirani

No new characters. No reboot. No multiverse gimmick. Just the same three men — played by **Aamir Khan**, **R Madhavan**, and **Sharman Joshi** — two decades older, navigating the part of life that nobody's idealism prepared them for. The part where "All is well" stops being a mantra and starts being a question.

Hirani and his long-time writing partner **Abhijat Joshi** are currently "locked up outside Mumbai" working on an early draft. **Aamir Khan** has read the initial story and signed on. "It's a beautiful story," Khan said in an earlier interview. "The script still needs some work, but the story itself is really good — unusual, with the same humour as the first film."

Will there be a message? "Of course," Hirani laughed. "A big one!"

## Why This Hits Different for the Diaspora

Here's the thing about *3 Idiots* and the Indian diaspora: the film didn't just reflect the pressure-cooker education system — it offered an escape from it. For the generation of NRIs who left India in the 2000s and 2010s, Rancho's refusal to play the game was aspirational in a way that landed harder abroad than at home. You were already the one who'd left. You'd already chosen a different path. Rancho validated that.

Now that same generation is pushing 40. They have kids of their own. They're navigating school admissions, career plateaus, marriages that require maintenance, and the quiet terror of becoming their parents. A *3 Idiots* sequel about mid-life crisis isn't just commercially smart — it's emotionally precise. Hirani knows exactly who his audience has become, because they grew up alongside his characters.

The original cast reunion adds weight. **R Madhavan** — fresh off a Padma Shri honour this week for his contributions to Indian cinema — brings a gravitas now that his younger self didn't have. **Sharman Joshi** has quietly built one of the most consistent careers in Hindi cinema. And **Aamir Khan**, whatever you think of his choices, still commands the kind of opening-weekend attention that no other Indian actor of his generation can match.

Expect **Kareena Kapoor Khan**, **Boman Irani**, and **Mona Singh** to return as well, though none have been formally confirmed beyond Hirani's statement that "all of them are the same characters."

## The Timeline

Hirani has been careful to manage expectations. The script is in early draft. He and Joshi expect to have a clearer picture of the production timeline "in the next two months." There's no release date, no shoot schedule, and no title beyond the working assumption that it'll carry the *3 Idiots* name.

But the fact that Aamir Khan is already involved — and enthusiastic — suggests this isn't a maybe. It's a when.

For a diaspora audience that grew up on this film and now finds itself exactly where Rancho, Farhan, and Raju are about to be — married, employed, mildly panicked, and wondering if this is really it — the sequel doesn't need to be announced.

It just needs to be honest.

"All is well" hits different at forty.
